chief_complaint: Worsening shortness of breath over the past week, particularly with exertion, and a persistent dry cough.
doctor_notes: Patient presents with symptoms suggestive of pneumonia. Chest X-ray shows infiltrates in the right lower lobe. Vital signs are stable but blood pressure is slightly elevated. Patient has a history of hypertension managed with Lisinopril. Initiated Azithromycin for pneumonia. Advised on rest, hydration, and to monitor symptoms closely. Follow-up in 1 week or sooner if symptoms worsen.

conversation_summary.speaker: Doctor
conversation_summary.text: Hello Eleanor, what brings you in today?

conversation_summary.speaker: Patient
conversation_summary.text: Doctor, I've been feeling so breathless lately, especially when I try to walk around the house. It started a few days ago and has gotten worse. I also have this nagging cough that just won't go away.

conversation_summary.speaker: Doctor
conversation_summary.text: I see. Have you had any fever, chills, or chest pain?

conversation_summary.speaker: Patient
conversation_summary.text: A slight fever yesterday, but it's gone now. No chest pain, thankfully.

conversation_summary.speaker: Doctor
conversation_summary.text: Okay, we'll need to get a chest X-ray and some blood work done to figure this out. I'll also check your blood pressure and listen to your lungs.

conversation_summary.speaker: Doctor
conversation_summary.text: The X-ray shows some inflammation in your lung, and your white blood cell count is a bit high, which is consistent with an infection. I'm prescribing you an antibiotic called Azithromycin to help clear this up. I'll also keep you on your Lisinopril for your blood pressure.

conversation_summary.speaker: Patient
conversation_summary.text: Thank you, Doctor. How long will it take for me to feel better?

conversation_summary.speaker: Doctor
conversation_summary.text: You should start feeling some improvement within a few days, but it's important to finish the entire course of antibiotics. Please rest, drink plenty of fluids, and if your breathing gets significantly worse or you develop a high fever, don't hesitate to call us or go to the emergency room.
